Has anyone had trouble with this, or are we just making this change because we can?

To me to seems incredibly confusing to give the users the option to set a rendering driver that we know doesn't exist. 

It's different with command line arguments because we can't give immediate feedback. With project settings, we can immediately tell the user that the value they input is invalid if the property accepts a string, or not provide the option if we can provide a fixed list.

> Has anyone had trouble with this, or are we just making this change because we can?
> 
> To me to seems incredibly confusing to give the users the option to set a rendering driver that we know doesn't exist.
> 
> It's different with command line arguments because we can't give immediate feedback. With project settings, we can immediately tell the user that the value they input is invalid if the property accepts a string, or not provide the option if we can provide a fixed list.

As I mentioned, it's not a conventional usage. In my own application, I provide a fixed list, but certain edge cases require users to manually modify the configuration file (for example, using `d3d12` in `wine`—the application runs, but the screen remains entirely black, which doesn't trigger a fallback to the rendering driver). If users choose to edit the configuration file manually, they should know what they're doing, and even if they make a mistake, they still have a chance to correct it. (Note: The users here are not Godot users but rather users of the application I developed using Godot.)

Even without this PR, the valid options still include `opengl3_x`, just as `RenderingServer.get_current_rendering_driver_name()` would return `opengl3_x`. However, directly setting `rendering/rendering_device/driver` to `opengl3_x` would cause a bug due to an incorrect `rendering/renderer/rendering_method`.

Currently, it indeed lacks a check. I can add one—should I?

> or not provide the option if we can provide a fixed list.

Note that the engine currently doesn't provide this list for projects to use, but https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/109247 makes it possible.

However, I believe this PR also falls under bug fixes. Currently, `rendering/rendering_device/driver` allows users to freely switch between `vulkan`, `d3d12`, or `opengl3_x`. When set to `opengl3_x`, the main window can render normally, but because `rendering/renderer/rendering_method` does not change to `gl_compatibility`, it causes rendering issues with child windows.
It looks like a check was canceled on its own, probably not an issue caused by a PR?

I understand the (niche) use case but this makes no sense sadly.

`rendering/rendering_device/driver` is the driver for RenderingDevice-based rendering methods, and `opengl3*` options are not valid for this. We shouldn't handle them.

Instructing your users to manually edit this specific setting to achieve an OpenGL fallback is just you giving users invalid instructions (or if they try it themselves, they're tinkering and should accept that not all combinations of random strings can work).

The use case is too niche for accepting this change IMO. You should instruct users to modify `rendering/renderer/rendering_method` if they want to use Compatibility, and `rendering/gl_compatibility/driver` if they want to set ANGLE or GL ES specifically.

I understand this technically works when using `--rendering-driver` which maps to both settings, but this is already very spaghetti code in `main.cpp` that's very error prone and leads to nasty situations such as this one. We shouldn't continue on that route.

I also agree that the usability of the various project settings for rendering method and drivers is pretty bad. But we couldn't come up to a better system before 4.0 and now we're stuck with it.

> `rendering/rendering_device/driver` is the driver for RenderingDevice-based rendering methods, and `opengl3*` options are not valid for this. We shouldn't handle them.

If `rendering/rendering_device/driver` should not allow `opengl3*`, then `--rendering-driver` should not allow `opengl3*` either.

> I understand the (niche) use case but this makes no sense sadly.

This is a real-world scenario and need that I have been using in my project for a long time, and `--rendering-driver` already allows `opengl3*`. I don't understand why you think it's meaningless.

> > `rendering/rendering_device/driver` is the driver for RenderingDevice-based rendering methods, and `opengl3*` options are not valid for this. We shouldn't handle them.
> 
> If `rendering/rendering_device/driver` should not allow `opengl3*`, then `--rendering-driver` should not allow `opengl3*` either.

`--rendering-driver` maps to either `rendering/rendering_device/driver` (for RenderingDevice based rendering methods) or `rendering/gl_compatibility/driver` (for the Compatibility rendering method). The project settings however are rendering method specific and shouldn't be muddied up.

So yes, `--rendering-driver` allows `opengl*` because it's meant to be used alongside `--rendering-method gl_compatibility` to specify the driver variant.

And it still works without `--rendering-method` as a convenience for debugging purposes, at the price of a lot of spaghetti code and tech debt which causes issues. But that's how it is, we shouldn't make it worse.

@scgm0 Please create a new branch and rebase that one instead of this PR. I've asked enough times that you should stop rebasing this daily. Alternatively, we can close this PR and you can continue rebasing its branch.

Besides the notification spam, this uses CI resources for absolutely no reason.

> I'd like to allow users to switch rendering APIs via override.cfg in my project.

Why are you telling your users to manually modify `override.cfg`? It should be handled by your project, you can normally write the file and restart to apply it.
Alternatively you can ship with batch/bash scripts that run the project with command line arguments.

> Why are you telling your users to manually modify `override.cfg`? It should be handled by your project, you can normally write the file and restart to apply it. Alternatively you can ship with batch/bash scripts that run the project with command line arguments.

Because this serves as the final safeguard for users, although I have provided rendering driver settings in the application, there are situations where the program runs normally but the screen fails to render correctly. In such cases, users can modify the rendering driver in `override.cfg` on their own to try if other drivers can render the screen properly.

Moreover, to facilitate distribution among users, my application only offers a single executable file, which is a crucial point for its dissemination in China.

As for why I don’t encourage users to run the program via `--rendering-device`, it’s because a vast number of average users have no idea what a terminal is or how to use the command line. The barrier to using the command line is much higher than developers tend to assume.

I am a developer, but I cannot view things solely from a developer’s perspective; I also need to consider the actual user experience.

That being said, this PR is indeed not perfect, so I have recreated it at https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/113162, where I standardized and organized what @akien-mga referred to as spaghetti code. It’s just that you haven’t reviewed it yet.

I understand that you don’t agree with the usage scenarios I described and are reluctant to merge my PR, which is why you keep expressing doubts instead of saying, as you do with PRs you favor, "Let’s merge it first and address other issues later." So be it. Unlike you, I don’t receive a salary from the Foundation, and no one provides financial support for these actions of mine. I simply don’t want to let down the users who have sponsored me in the past.

> I am a developer, but I cannot view things solely from a developer’s perspective; I also need to consider the actual user experience.

I agree with that, but IIUC the current user experience you offer is that non-developers are asked to create an `override.cfg` file themselves and then write some convoluted TOML-like code to achieve some configuration.
And they need to understand the difference between `opengl3`, `opengl3_angle`, `opengl3_es`...

I assume you must have lengthy documentation on how they should be doing that, at which point telling them to copy two lines instead of one probably doesn't worse the user experience. And they need to find your documentation, likely after having their game crash on start, so that also doesn't sound like a great experience.

You could even provide pre-configured `override.cfg` files for different scenarios (running on compatibility with ANGLE, etc.).

I admit I'm not familiar enough with the Chinese market to judge whether the approach is good or not. But if a single .exe is mandatory, I would recommend making a single .exe installer (could be a self-extracting zip) that includes a bunch of `.bat` scripts to run the game with various options, and a README that tells users what to try if the main .exe/.bat crashes / where to find support.

> Unlike you, I don’t receive a salary from the Foundation, and no one provides financial support for these actions of mine. 

This is totally uncalled for, who gets paid by whom is irrelevant to reviewing whether a solution is correct or a use case worth supporting.

> That being said, this PR is indeed not perfect, so I have recreated it at https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/113162, where I standardized and organized what @akien-mga referred to as spaghetti code. It’s just that you haven’t reviewed it yet.

Let's review that PR indeed. This one won't be merged so let's close it (you can then still rebase it in your fork as you used to to keep using it in production).
